newsitem.title: USA: Indian tribe files suit against Detroit casinos.
newsitem.headline: Indian tribe files suit against Detroit casinos.

text.p: An Indian tribe Wednesday filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Michigan claiming a Nov 5 state-wide referendum allowing casinos in Detroit was "illegal and unconstitutional."

The lawsuit, filed in Grand Rapids by the Lac Vieux Desert Band of the Lake Superior Chippewa Indians, seeks injunctive relief from the court to stop the implementation of Proposal E, the referendum which allowed for three casinos in Detroit.
The lawsuit claims that under the provisions of Proposal E, special preferences were given to two groups for three available casino operating licenses.

The Lac Vieux Desert tribe is asking the court to rule that the two license preferences are illegal. The tribe also claims that both a federal court order and a compact with the state allows tribes to exclusively operate electronic games of chance in Michigan.

"The intention of our lawsuit is not to necessarily stop casino gaming in Detroit, but to be part of it," said Tribal Chairman John McGeshick, in a news release. "Indian tribes have been granted the exclusive right by the state and federal governments to operate casino gaming in Michigan, and any measure which takes away this right is illegal and unconstitutional."

Tuesday, the State Gaming Control board proposed removing the casino license preferences for two local groups that backed Proposal E due to constitutional concerns, according to John Truscott, spokesman for Michigan Gov. John Engler.

Truscott said that legislation would be introduced to eliminate preferential treatment and to hopefully head off the tribe's lawsuit. He added that a two-thirds vote of the legislature would be required to make the change.

He also disagreed with the tribe's contention they have an exclusive right to gaming in the state, saying that exclusivity only applies to the financial arrangement that allows the state to capture a percentage of Indian gaming revenues.

The Lac Vieux Desert tribe also announced Wednesday that if it is denied the opportunity to operate a casino in Detroit, it would seek to establish a gambling operation elsewhere in the Detroit area, possibly at the Pontiac Silverdome.
McGeshick said the Silverdome, which is slated to loose its major tenant, the Detroit Lions football team, to a new stadium in Detroit, would "make a fine gaming facility."
Truscott said that given Engler's power to veto any off-reservation casinos in the state, the governor would oppose any move to operate an Indian-run casino at the Silverdome.
The Lac Vieux Desert Indians currently operate a casino on a 200-acre reservation just over a mile north of Watersmeet near the Wisconsin border in Michigan's upper peninsula.
A spokesman for Detroit Mayor Dennis Archer had no immediate comment on the tribe's announcement.

Under Proposal E, Detroit would receive 55 percent of revenues generated from an 18 percent tax on the three city casinos. The rest of the revenues would be deposited in the state's K-12 School Aid Fund.
